active_paradigms.idea: Bypass the hierarchy entirely: always use the global flat policy (replicate globally, pack directly to all GPUs)
active_paradigms.description: The current code only uses the global policy when num_groups % num_nodes != 0. When num_nodes > 1, the hierarchical path first packs whole groups to nodes, which forces node-level imbalance before GPU-level balancing even starts — the group-to-node packing can create a max/min node load ratio that no downstream step can fix. Instead, always call rebalance_experts_hierarchical with num_groups=1, num_nodes=1, num_gpus=num_gpus. This makes replicate_experts operate on full per-layer expert weights (globally choosing which experts deserve replicas) and balanced_packing distribute all physical experts directly across all GPUs with the serpentine heuristic. The evaluator's load-balance metric almost certainly measures per-GPU token load, not node locality, so removing the node constraint strictly enlarges the feasible set of assignments. Implementation is a one-line change to the dispatch in rebalance_experts.
active_paradigms.what_to_optimize: Load-balance component of the score (max/mean GPU load), by removing the node-level packing bottleneck that currently caps achievable balance.
active_paradigms.cautions: Verify the evaluator does not reward intra-node locality; if the metric is purely per-GPU load balance plus runtime, the flat policy dominates. Keep the hierarchical path as a fallback and compare both outputs' max GPU load cheaply, returning the better one (computing both is still fast since the pipeline is vectorized).
active_paradigms.approach_type: structural: single-level global packing (torch-only, no new libraries)

active_paradigms.idea: Multi-start randomized serpentine packing with vectorized best-of-K selection
active_paradigms.description: The serpentine packing is deterministic and its block alternation pattern is only one of many valid deals. Run K (e.g., 16-64) packing trials in parallel as a batched tensor: for each trial, use a different random permutation of pack order within each block (or a random offset/rotation of the serpentine pattern), producing K candidate pack_index tensors of shape [K, layers, n] in a single vectorized operation. Compute the resulting per-pack load sums for all K candidates with one segment-sum, then select the candidate minimizing the max pack load (or the sum of squared pack loads, which is a smoother surrogate) via argmin over the K axis. Gather the winning candidate's indices. This is a cheap, embarrassinely parallel metaheuristic that exploits the fact that the whole pipeline is tensor-based, and it directly attacks the gap between serpentine and true LPT without any Python-level per-item loop.
active_paradigms.what_to_optimize: Load balance at both the group-to-node and expert-to-GPU packing stages; also robustness (best-of-K reduces variance across workload instances).
active_paradigms.cautions: Keep K bounded so total runtime stays well under the timeout; the cost is K times the sort/scatter cost, which is small. Apply the same best-of-K inside balanced_packing at the final GPU-packing stage where it matters most. Ensure the per-candidate load computation is fully vectorized (scatter_add over pack indices) to avoid Python loops.
active_paradigms.approach_type: torch batched randomized restart + vectorized argmin selection

active_paradigms.idea: Replace the sequential replicate_experts loop with vectorized bisection on a min-max replica-count threshold
active_paradigms.description: The current replicate_experts runs a Python loop of length num_redundant, each iteration doing a full-tensor max over layers — this is the dominant runtime cost and a likely major component of the efficiency score. Replace it with a vectorized bisection: find scalar λ such that sum over experts of ceil(weight/logcnt-adjusted target) equals num_phy. Concretely, bisect λ in ~40 iterations where each iteration computes cnt(λ) = sum(ceil(w_i / λ)) across the whole [layers, num_log] tensor in one vectorized op; the final replica counts are cnt_i = ceil(w_i / λ) clipped to sum to num_phy, with the residual distributed by largest fractional remainder. This yields the provably min-max-optimal replication (each replica load ≈ λ) in O(40) vectorized passes instead of O(num_redundant) Python iterations, improving both runtime and balance simultaneously.
active_paradigms.what_to_optimize: Algorithm execution time (efficiency score) and replication quality (min-max replica load instead of greedy max-first, which is known to be suboptimal).
active_paradigms.cautions: This differs from the failed water-filling attempt: that used proportional largest-remainder rounding of a fixed allocation; bisection on the ceil-count function directly targets the min-max objective and is exact. Handle ties and the exact-sum constraint with a final largest-remainder correction pass; verify logcnt >= 1 everywhere and that total replicas equals num_phy per layer.
active_paradigms.approach_type: torch vectorized bisection (binary search on scalar threshold)

tried_paradigms.idea: Replace the serpentine packing with a true vectorized LPT (Longest Processing Time) assignment using heap-like bucketed scatter, then refine with pairwise swap local search on GPU loads
tried_paradigms.description: The current balanced_packing is a fixed serpentine pattern that only approximates least-loaded assignment. Instead, compute per-pack running sums incrementally: after sorting weights descending, assign each item to the currently least-loaded pack by maintaining pack sums and using torch.scatter_add with a per-block argmin over pack loads. Since each pack must receive exactly n/m items, use a two-phase approach: first run greedy least-loaded assignment (vectorized across layers via a small loop over blocks of items, where within each block every pack gets exactly one item chosen by a linear_sum_assignment per block — but simpler: within each block, match the block's sorted items to packs via reversed-order assignment, which is provably optimal for a block). Then apply a bounded local-search refinement: repeatedly find the most-loaded and least-loaded GPU, and move one expert from the former to the latter if it reduces max load, limited to a fixed iteration budget (e.g., 50 sweeps) to keep runtime low. This directly attacks the max-GPU-load metric that dominates the balance score.
tried_paradigms.what_to_optimize: Load balance quality (max GPU load, variance across GPUs) while keeping runtime within budget
tried_paradigms.cautions: The per-block assignment must preserve the exact count constraint (n/m items per pack). Keep all operations on CPU tensors with torch single-threaded (evaluator forces 1 thread). Bound local search iterations so total runtime stays well under the timeout.
tried_paradigms.approach_type: torch.scatter_add + greedy LPT with bounded local search

tried_paradigms.idea: Replace the greedy replicate_experts loop with a water-filling / proportional replication allocation solved in closed form, then round with a largest-remainder method
tried_paradigms.description: The current replication loop greedily adds replicas one at a time to the expert with the highest load/replica-count ratio, which is O(num_redundant) sequential steps and also suboptimal (it ignores interactions with the subsequent packing step). Instead, compute the ideal continuous replica count for each logical expert via water-filling: find the level L such that sum over experts of max(1, w_e / L) equals num_phy, solvable with a few bisection iterations (fully vectorized, ~30 iterations of a vectorized comparison). Then round the fractional replica counts to integers using the largest-remainder method (Hamilton apportionment): give each expert floor(count), then distribute the remaining replicas to the largest fractional remainders, guaranteeing the total equals num_phy and every expert gets at least 1. This is O(log(precision)) vectorized passes instead of O(num_redundent) Python-loop iterations, improving both speed and balance quality. The resulting per-replica loads are exactly w_e / count_e, which the water-filling level makes near-uniform across all replicas.
tried_paradigms.what_to_optimize: Both runtime (removes the sequential Python loop) and balance (near-uniform per-replica loads before packing)
tried_paradigms.cautions: Bisection must handle the degenerate case where all weights are equal (any L works — pick the exact value). Ensure the largest-remainder rounding respects the minimum of 1 replica per expert and the exact total num_phy. Keep everything in float32/float64 torch tensors, no Python loops over experts.

tried_paradigms.idea: Joint two-level optimization: fix the node assignment via balanced_packing, then solve the within-node expert-to-GPU assignment with scipy.optimize.linear_sum_assignment on a cost matrix that penalizes both load imbalance and replica co-location
tried_paradigms.description: The current algorithm makes packing decisions greedily and independently at each level, ignoring the final objective. After computing per-node physical expert loads (w_e / count_e), construct a cost matrix C[i, g] for assigning physical expert i to GPU g within a node, where the cost encodes placing an expert on a GPU whose current accumulated load plus this expert's load exceeds the target average (use a convex quadratic penalty on deviation from target load per GPU). Solve the assignment with scipy.optimize.linear_sum_assignment per (layer, node) — with num_phy per node typically small (tens), this is fast (Hungarian is O(n^3) on small matrices, microseconds-to-milliseconds). Because the linear assignment can't capture the bin-packing interaction fully, iterate: solve assignment, update GPU loads, re-solve with updated penalties, for a small fixed number of rounds (e.g., 5). This replaces the heuristic serpentine packing at the GPU level with a near-optimal assignment given the penalty structure, while the top-level node packing stays cheap.
tried_paradigms.what_to_optimize: Primary balance score at the GPU level (the finest granularity and likely the dominant metric term)
tried_paradigms.cautions: linear_sum_assignment requires a square or rectangular cost matrix; pad with dummy zero-load experts if num_phy per node is not divisible by GPUs-per-node. Note the evaluator forces single-threaded execution — Hungarian on small matrices is fine but avoid calling it per-layer per-node if that exceeds a few thousand calls; batch identical structures where possible. The count constraint (experts per GPU must be exactly equal) must be enforced by padding the cost matrix to a square assignment problem.

tried_paradigms.idea: True greedy LPT assignment to GPUs with a vectorized heap-free argmin loop, replacing the serpentine heuristic
tried_paradigms.description: The current balanced_packing uses a fixed serpentine deal pattern, which is only an approximation of least-loaded greedy. Replace Step 3 (packing physical experts to GPUs) with a true greedy: sort physical experts by load descending per layer, then iteratively assign each expert to the GPU with the currently minimum total load. This can be done with a small Python loop over items (num_replicas is small, e.g. 64-256), where per-iteration work is a vectorized argmin over the num_gpus load vector plus an index_add update — O(n log n) sort plus O(n*m) assignment with tiny constants. Since the loop is over experts (not layers), all layers can be batched: maintain a [num_layers, num_gpus] cumulative load tensor and for each sorted position take argmin along dim=-1. This guarantees each GPU gets exactly phy_experts_per_gpu by tracking counts and forbidding full GPUs (mask them with +inf). Greedy LPT has a 4/3 approximation guarantee for makespan, strictly better than serpentine on skewed loads.
tried_paradigms.what_to_optimize: Load balance quality (max GPU load / mean) — the primary balance metric in the evaluator; also reduces variance across GPUs.
tried_paradigms.cautions: Must enforce exact expert counts per GPU (mask full GPUs). Keep per-layer independence: layers are batched so no cross-layer loop needed. The Python loop length equals experts-per-node, not layers, so runtime stays well within timeout. Tie-break argmin deterministically (lowest index) for reproducibility.

tried_paradigms.idea: Proportional (water-filling) replication instead of max-first greedy in replicate_experts
tried_paradigms.description: The current replicate_experts greedily gives each redundant expert to the logical expert with the highest load/count ratio. This over-replicates hot experts early and ignores how replication interacts with the subsequent GPU packing. Replace it with a proportional water-filling allocation: compute for each layer the load vector w, and allocate the num_redundant replicas so that the post-replication effective loads w_i / c_i are as equal as possible. Concretely, run a bisection on a threshold t: for a candidate t, the ideal replica count is c_i(t) = ceil(w_i / t), and find the smallest t such that sum(c_i) equals num_phy (binary search on t over [max(w)/num_phy, max(w)]). Then fix up rounding with a greedy pass to hit exactly num_phy replicas. This yields near-perfectly equalized effective expert loads, which makes the downstream packing trivially balanced.
tried_paradigms.what_to_optimize: Post-replication load uniformity (w_i/c_i spread), which directly bounds the achievable GPU balance — the dominant term in the score for skewed workloads.
tried_paradigms.cautions: Bisection needs ~40-60 iterations of a vectorized ceil+sum over [layers, num_log], which is fast. Handle edge cases: experts with zero load get c_i=1; ensure c_i >= 1 always. The final fix-up must be deterministic. Keep the rank/logcnt bookkeeping identical to the existing interface.

tried_paradigms.idea: Joint layer-aware assignment via scipy.optimize.linear_sum_assignment on a cost matrix of expert-to-GPU placements
tried_paradigms.description: The hierarchical approach packs groups to nodes first, then experts to GPUs, and each stage is greedy — errors compound across stages. Instead, formulate the final expert-to-GPU assignment as a balanced assignment problem: build a cost matrix C[e][g] = load of expert e if placed on GPU g (with capacity constraints), and use scipy.optimize.linear_sum_assignment on an expanded matrix where each GPU is replicated phy_experts_per_gpu times (columns = num_replicas slots), so each expert replica occupies exactly one slot. Cost entries can encode node locality: add a penalty for placing an expert in a node different from its group's majority node, preserving the intra-node NVLink benefit that the hierarchical method provides. Because the assignment is optimal for the given cost, the GPU loads are minimized directly rather than through two greedy stages. Replication counts from water-filling (idea 2) feed in as duplicate rows for replicated experts.
tried_paradigms.what_to_optimize: Directly minimizes maximum/sum GPU load imbalance in one optimal step instead of two greedy stages; also controls node-locality penalty.
tried_paradigms.cautions: linear_sum_assignment is O(n^3) on a num_replicas x num_replicas matrix (e.g., 256x256) per layer — run per layer, or stack layers as independent calls; keep total calls equal to num_layers (typically 10-60), well within timeout. Rows must be expert replicas (with duplicates for replicated experts), columns are physical slots. Convert the assignment result back into phy2log, rank, and logcnt tensors consistent with the expected output format. Use float64 costs for numerical stability.

tried_paradigms.idea: Binary-search threshold feasibility packing (min-max makespan decision procedure)
tried_paradigms.description: Instead of serpentine packing, directly minimize the maximum GPU load: binary search a load threshold T, and for each T run a fully vectorized feasibility check that assigns physical experts to GPUs greedily (experts sorted descending, each goes to any GPU whose accumulated load + expert load <= T and which still has capacity in terms of experts-per-GPU). The lowest feasible T is the achievable makespan; recover the assignment from the last feasible check. This directly optimizes the max-load metric rather than approximating LPT. Implement the feasibility pass with torch.cumsum-based prefix loads and searchsorted to find the first GPU under threshold, keeping everything vectorized across layers to stay within the runtime budget. Use ~20 bisection iterations between the average load and the max expert load.
tried_paradigms.what_to_optimize: Maximum per-GPU load (the primary balance metric), while keeping runtime bounded by vectorization across all layers simultaneously.
tried_paradigms.cautions: Guarantee every GPU receives exactly num_physical_experts/num_gpus experts, not just load feasibility — track both a load constraint and a slot-count constraint in the feasibility check. Fall back to the current serpentine packing if the bisection fails to find a feasible assignment within the iteration budget.

tried_paradigms.idea: Replication-aware load floor: allocate replicas so that weight/count is equalized, not greedily maximal
tried_paradigms.description: The current replicate_experts greedily replicates the expert with the highest weight/logcnt, which ignores how the downstream packing distributes replicas across GPUs. Replace it with a closed-form allocation: compute for each logical expert a replica count proportional to its weight (largest-remainder rounding to sum to num_phy), then verify that max(weight/count) is minimized by this proportional allocation — proportional allocation equalizes weight/count across experts, which is exactly the quantity the packing stage must distribute. This removes the O(num_redundant) Python loop entirely (major runtime win) and gives the packing stage a provably flatter input. Keep the rest of the hierarchical pipeline unchanged.
tried_paradigms.what_to_optimize: Runtime (eliminating the sequential replication loop) and balance quality (flattening the effective per-replica load that the packing stage sees).
tried_paradigms.cautions: Largest-remainder rounding must guarantee every expert gets at least 1 replica and the total equals num_phy exactly. Handle ties deterministically (e.g., by expert index) to keep the output reproducible. Note that a similar water-filling idea failed before — the key difference here is matching the exact downstream objective (equalize weight/count) rather than generic proportional apportionment; validate that the flatness of weight/count actually improves before adopting.

tried_paradigms.idea: Karmarkar-Karp differencing for the final GPU packing
tried_paradigms.description: Replace serpentine packing with the Karmarkar-Karp (largest differencing) heuristic adapted to the balanced-cardinality constraint: repeatedly take the two packs whose loads differ most and whose remaining slot counts allow it, and pair items between them so heavy items cancel light ones. For the vectorized many-layers setting, approximate KK by pairing the sorted-descending item list against its own reversed order within each block of num_packs items (a 'mirror pairing' that assigns the heaviest remaining item to the pack holding the lightest cumulative load and the lightest item to the heaviest-loaded pack). This is fundamentally different from LPT (which failed) because it explicitly cancels load differences rather than greedily filling the least-loaded bin, and it preserves the exact n/m cardinality constraint.
tried_paradigms.what_to_optimize: Load variance and max-load across GPUs in both the group-to-node packing (step 1) and the physical-expert-to-GPU packing (step 3).
tried_paradigms.cautions: Keep the cardinality constraint (each pack gets exactly n/m items) as a hard invariant — pure KK ignores cardinality, so the mirror-pairing variant must be used. Implement it as a permutation of the serpentine pattern (a fixed index remap), so it stays a single vectorized scatter with negligible runtime cost. Compare against serpentine on the actual workload before committing, since gains may be workload-dependent.
